Camping vs Hotels: The Motorcycle Tourer's Dilemma

It's the great debate of motorcycle touring. Do you strap a tent to the back and embrace the wild, or book a comfortable B&B and arrive to a hot shower and a proper bed? Both have passionate advocates, and both have genuine advantages. Let's break it down honestly.

The Case for Camping

Freedom and flexibility: With a tent, you're never tied to a booking. Found an incredible spot? Stop and camp. Weather turns? Find shelter and wait it out. This flexibility is camping's greatest strength, especially on tours where plans change daily.

Cost: Campsites in the UK range from £8-20 per night. Wild camping in Scotland is free and legal under the right-to-roam. Over a week-long tour, camping can save you £300-500 compared to B&Bs and hotels.

The experience: Waking up to the sound of a river, brewing coffee as the mist lifts off a Highland loch, watching the sunset from your tent door. These moments are uniquely available to touring campers and they stay with you forever.

The Case for Hotels and B&Bs

Comfort and recovery: After 200 miles on twisting roads, a proper bed, a hot bath, and a cooked breakfast are restorative in a way a sleeping mat simply can't match. You'll ride better the next day for a good night's sleep.

Less to carry: Without camping gear, your luggage is lighter and more compact. The bike handles better, packing is faster, and you need less luggage capacity overall. A tail bag might be all you need.

Security: Your gear is locked inside a building rather than sitting in a tent by the roadside. For expensive electronics and riding kit, this peace of mind matters.

Local knowledge: B&B owners in touring areas are often riders themselves or at least know the best local roads. The route tips you'll pick up over breakfast are invaluable.

Cost Comparison (Per Night)

  • Wild camping (Scotland): Free
  • Basic campsite: £8-15
  • Campsite with facilities: £15-25
  • Budget B&B: £40-60
  • Mid-range B&B/pub room: £60-90
  • Hotel: £80-150+
  • Bothy (Scotland): Free (donation encouraged)

The Hybrid Approach

Most experienced tourers end up with a hybrid strategy, and this is what we'd recommend for UK touring:

  • Camp when the weather is good and you're in scenic locations
  • Book a B&B when you need a rest, laundry, or the forecast is terrible
  • Use bothies in Scotland for a unique free experience
  • Treat yourself to a nice hotel for the last night as a reward
The hybrid approach gives you the best of both worlds. Pack camping gear for flexibility, but don't be afraid to ditch the tent for a comfortable night when you need it. There's no shame in comfort.

Packing Implications

If you decide to camp, you'll need an additional 8-12 litres of luggage space for:

  • Tent (2-3kg packed)
  • Sleeping bag and mat (2-3kg combined)
  • Cooking setup (1-2kg if using a compact stove)

This typically means upgrading from a tail bag to a pannier system, or at least adding a dry bag bungeed to the pillion seat.

Our Verdict

For a first tour, go with B&Bs. You'll learn what you actually need without the added complexity of camping logistics. For experienced tourers, carry camping gear for the option but don't commit to camping every night. The UK is a small island with incredible variety — embrace all of it. faq.q: How much can camping save on a week-long tour?
faq.a: Camping can save you £300 to £500 over a week compared with B&Bs and hotels. UK campsites range from £8 to £20 per night, and wild camping in Scotland is free and legal under the right-to-roam. Bothies are also free, with a donation encouraged, making Scotland the cheapest place to tour.

faq.q: Is wild camping legal in the UK?
faq.a: Wild camping is legal in Scotland under the Scottish Outdoor Access Code, provided you camp away from roads and buildings and leave no trace. In England and Wales it generally requires the landowner's permission, apart from limited areas such as parts of Dartmoor, so plan accordingly if you are heading south.

faq.q: What extra luggage does camping require?
faq.a: Camping typically adds 8 to 12 litres of luggage space for a tent (2 to 3kg packed), sleeping bag and mat (2 to 3kg combined) and a compact cooking setup (1 to 2kg). This usually means upgrading from a tail bag to a pannier system, or at least bungeeing a dry bag to the pillion seat.

Most experienced tourers camp when the weather is good and they are in scenic locations, then book a B&B when they need a rest, laundry or the forecast is terrible. Use bothies in Scotland for a free, unique experience and treat yourself to a nice hotel on the last night. It gives you the best of both worlds.

faq.q: Which is better for a first tour?
faq.a: For a first tour, go with B&Bs. You will learn what you actually need without the added complexity of camping logistics, and arriving to a hot shower and a proper bed helps you ride better the next day. Once you have a few tours behind you, carry camping gear for the option without committing to it every night.
